segments.text: **Speech: 6**

**Hon. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi:** Hon. Speaker, on the demand for grants for the Large Industries Department, many members belonging to the Opposition and allied parties have given good explanations and constructive suggestions so that industry may grow further in Tamil Nadu. Following those views, and having obtained the opportunity that this Government has so far taken up in the industrial field, I now stand before this House.

First, our Legislative Assembly member and Tamil Maanila Congress member Thiru Alagiri, when he began speaking on this grant, said that he was speaking with a heavy heart and said that, like him, I too would be heavy-hearted. Perhaps, because we are going to speak about heavy industries, the word “heavy” found a place in his mind. As far as I am concerned, I am not one who ever wishes to make my heart heavy, nor have I done so. For, when Anna passed away, I asked him to lend me his heart. (Sound of desk-thumping.) It is with that heart which can bear anything that I have conducted my public life, particularly my political life.
In the film *Poompuhar*, I wrote the dialogue, “Only when conscience sleeps does the monkey-mind set out to roam the town.” If not only I, but everyone begins to think about that—
truth will not remain in darkness for long; it will come into the light. Just as darkness cannot keep covering the sun forever, and just as dawn must somehow come, truth too must emerge.

In this demand for grants, the two points made by Thiru Alagiri and by Thiru Abdul Latheef, leader of the Indian National League, are acceptable points. Although Thiru Abdul Latheef placed before us more political views than views about the industrial sector, he pointed out that, whatever our condition and wherever we may stand, we remain on the path of working for a secular Government to be formed in India and for democratic rule to continue. Therefore, I am duty-bound to convey my thanks to dear Thiru Alagiri, who opened the debate, and to my dear friend Thiru Abdul Latheef, who followed him with a few observations.

Speaking about industry, Thiru Mani, who spoke on behalf of the Marxist Communist Party, and Thiru Subbarayan, who spoke on behalf of the Communist Party of India, stressed that public-sector undertakings in Tamil Nadu should be encouraged further and said that this Government should take the necessary steps. We should not forget that the policy note for this demand for grants itself states that 13 public-sector undertakings are now functioning in Tamil Nadu with investments exceeding Rs. 20,000 crore, and that the Tamil Nadu Government will press the Central Government to immediately undertake expansion and production-capacity enhancement work worth about Rs. 16,000 crore in various public-sector undertakings such as the Neyveli lignite mines, Chennai Oil Refinery, Salem Steel Plant and Indian Rare Earths.

Therefore, under the new economic policy we have accepted, while encouraging private industries, everyone can have confidence that, along with the Joint Sector and Associate Sector already created by the Kazhagam Government, the public sector too will certainly be given a proper place.

Thiru Alagiri said that, on the question of exports, we are at a very “next” stage. In particular, he cited newsprint exports and said that this year they are Rs. 10 crore lower than last year. That is true. Because the price of newsprint abroad is very low, interest in exports has declined. Not only that, an editorial on exports appeared in *The Hindu* on 19-4-1997. It stated that in 1996-97 the volume handled in the world export-import market had fallen from 6 per cent to 4 per cent, according to World Trade Organisation (W.T.O.) statistics; that the value of merchandise trade in 1995-96 was 5,100 billion dollars; that growth in export trade had fallen from 14 per cent to 5 per cent this year; that exports had especially declined in Asia; that exports of industrially developed countries such as Japan, Taiwan and South Korea had also fallen considerably; and that, in India in particular, efforts had been made to reach the export target of 7 per cent, while 6 per cent had been achieved.
Tamil Nadu’s exports are also at this level; exports and imports in the world market have fallen sharply; India’s exports too have not risen in the specified—

manner. Even so, exports from Tamil Nadu have not suffered a percentage decline at the world level. Nevertheless, every step will be taken to increase exports, and I am duty-bound to give that reply to the point made by Thiru Alagiri and others.

We must also not forget that 16 per cent of India’s total exports are made from Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu’s population is only 6 per cent of India’s total population, but 16 per cent of India’s total exports are made from Tamil Nadu. In particular, ‘cotton yarn’, ‘textiles’, leather goods and banians are among the articles exported.

Thiru Alagiri made another allegation about the ‘SIPCOT’ organisation. He said that it was behaving very miserly, like ‘Shylock’, and that it had acted in an extremely miserly fashion in demanding repayment of a loan given to a Cuddalore company called ‘Coromandel Polybags’. When I asked for the details, I was informed that SIPCOT had lent Rs. 45.50 lakh to the Coromandel company. With interest added to that Rs. 45 lakh, the total had become Rs. 117 lakh. Since the company had not paid so far, SIPCOT had to take legal action, conduct an auction and take steps to recover SIPCOT’s money. Therefore, SIPCOT did not deliberately act in a miserly fashion: the money lent was not repaid, interest was not paid, and even the amount agreed to in settlement talks was not paid. Therefore—
it was only in that situation of non-payment that the organisation had to take legal action, which I am duty-bound to point out.

As far as Tamil Nadu is concerned, a false campaign is going on in the country, turning into a question mark whether industry grew under Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam rule and claiming that it did not. I believe that the few explanations I can give will hurt no one. When the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam came to office in 1967, we not only pressed the Central Government to expand public-sector projects already functioning in Tamil Nadu, such as the Tuticorin Port project and Neyveli Lignite Corporation, to increase production and expand employment, but the State Government also provided all necessary facilities for such arrangements. The country knows very well that it was the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government which continuously fought with the Central Government and paved the way for a second mine to be opened at Neyveli and for the Salem Steel Plant to be established.

No one can forget that the ‘SPIC’ fertiliser factory at Tuticorin, which today has grown to a level praised by countries across the world and may be valued at one or two thousand crore rupees, was established during Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam rule.

Similarly, during Kazhagam rule, with the view that public-sector factories alone could not expand industrial development in Tamil Nadu, steps were taken to encourage and motivate interested entrepreneurs, establish industrial estates, allot land at low cost and provide—

loan assistance needed for industrial projects together with a capital subsidy — ‘Capital Subsidy’. It was the Kazhagam Government that created the new institution State Industries Promotion Corporation of Tamil Nadu — ‘SIPCOT’ — in 1971. Thereafter, SIPCOT established industrial complexes in which all basic facilities required for industrial growth could be provided in one place. Hon. members know very well that Ranipet was one such place.

In 1973, on 729.78 acres, 107 industrial units involving an investment of Rs. 168 crore were created there during Kazhagam rule. When the Kazhagam assumed office, we heard about that site at Ranipet. My friend Thiru Madhavan was then Industries Minister and brought the matter to my attention. The information was that the site had already been purchased during Congress rule for setting up an industrial estate, but because the estate had not been established there, the preceding Congress Government had thought of selling the land or abandoning the idea. He said we should visit the site. I, the Industries Minister of that day, and other officials went to Ranipet, inspected the place and decided that there was no need to sell it or give it away and that SIPCOT itself could establish an industrial undertaking there. The result was that on that roughly 730-acre area, 107 industrial units involving Rs. 168 crore of investment were established even then.

Similarly, at Hosur in 1974, during Kazhagam rule, we created 186 industrial units with investment exceeding Rs. 500 crore and employment for 20,000 people. This too was during Kazhagam rule. With a plan to increase industrial development in backward parts of Tamil Nadu, industrial complexes were created on 225 acres at Manamadurai and on 10 acres at Pudukkottai. Apart from these, the Kazhagam Government of that time, through SIPCOT, encouraged private efforts to establish industrial complexes in backward areas such as Anaikaranpatti in Ramanathapuram district. These are factual truths.
Following this, it was also the Kazhagam Government that started ‘SIDCO’ in 1971 to support and assist small industries.

With the objective of encouraging small-industry growth in Tamil Nadu, the Small Industries Development Corporation — ‘SIDCO’ — was established. Likewise, ‘TIDCO’ had already been created in 1965 during Congress rule. Under that organisation, a change was made during Kazhagam rule so that industries could be established in the Joint Sector, with a Government share of 26 per cent, and in the Associate Sector, with a Government share of 11 per cent. These two sectors began to be implemented jointly with TIDCO, and many industries were established in Tamil Nadu.

Similarly, it was in 1972 that the Tamil Nadu Electronics Corporation — ‘ELCOT’ — with a long-term plan that electronics industries should prosper in Tamil Nadu, created an electronics division in the office of the Director of Industries and Commerce in 1972 and, in connection with it, established various industrial divisions. Electronic Corporation of Tamil Nadu was established in 1975 under the abbreviated name ‘ELCOT’—
which I am duty-bound to place before the members of the House.

Today ELCOT has grown, and electronics industrial divisions throughout Tamil Nadu have developed to a scale of nearly Rs. 200 crore, which I am happy to inform the House. By creating institutions such as SIPCOT, SIDCO and ELCOT, the Kazhagam Government paved the way for industries to grow on a large scale in Tamil Nadu. It began helping entrepreneurs by encouraging them and enabling them to obtain credit freely. By granting tax exemptions, deferring sales-tax collection, giving electricity-tariff concessions and providing many other forms of assistance, the Kazhagam Government helped new industries come into being in Tamil Nadu.

In 1975, a legislator from Western Australia, Thiru William Vithas, visited Tamil Nadu and returned home. After returning, he spoke in the Western Australian Legislature about industrial development in Tamil Nadu. He said that the Tamil Nadu Government had many attractive ideas for assisting factories; that the Government was making great efforts to start factories in Tamil Nadu and was also giving various concessions; that those concessions included no tax for two years for any foreign factory started in Tamil Nadu and electricity-tariff concessions during the growth period of new factories. He said he regarded these as excellent measures and requested that, when planning for industrial development in his country, that is, in Western—

Australia, all these matters should be taken into account. His open appreciation was reported in the newspapers even then. (Sound of desk-thumping.) Thus, we expanded industrial development to a level that was praised not only in India but also by foreigners. In particular, as I mentioned at the outset, I ask you to consider the factories our Government created through the Joint Sector alone.
1. At Tuticorin, SPIC — Southern Petro Chemicals Industries Corporation Limited.
2. The Tuticorin Alkali Chemicals factory producing ‘soda ash’ and ammonium chloride using surplus ammonia from SPIC.
3. Tamil Nadu Chemical Process Limited, Karaikudi, producing sodium hydrosulphite used in the ‘box dyes’ required by the textile industry.
4. Tamil Nadu Chromates and Chemical Limited at the Ranipet industrial estate, producing chromium sulphate, sodium dichromate and sodium sulphate needed by dye factories in South India.
5. Pandian Chemicals Limited at Narasingampatti in Melur taluk, Madurai district, producing potassium chloride.
6. Tamil Nadu Chlorine Alide Chemicals Limited at Manalur in the old Ramanathapuram district, producing aluminium chloride.
7. Tamil Nadu Tata Pharmaceuticals at Pallavaram, manufacturing medicines.
8. Dynavision Limited at Adyar, manufacturing television sets.
9. Marthik Crystal Salt factory in the Kovalam area, producing industrial salt.
10. Asia Tobacco Company near Hosur.
11. An ocean-going large trawler-building factory in the Mandapam area for building fishing boats.
12. Tamil Nadu Alkaline Batteries Limited at the Ambattur industrial estate.
13. Asian Bearings Limited near Hosur.
14. A casting foundry at Arakkonam.
15. Indar Continental Leathers Limited, manufacturing glove leather, garments, leather, upper leather and similar products.
I am duty-bound to inform the House that these took shape as Joint Sector industries.
After that the Government was dismissed. I now wish to point out to Hon. members the arrangements made after 13 years, during Kazhagam rule in 1989-90, to make industrial development flourish.
You know the North Chennai Thermal Power Station. Sites had been considered for it and the project was initially estimated at Rs. 500 crore. Because no one agreed to acquisition of the site—

and because litigation went all the way to the Supreme Court, the land had not been acquired by the Government when the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government assumed office in 1989. Immediately after taking office, we called the owners of the site, spoke to them and obtained their agreement, and no one can forget that the then President of India was invited to conduct the commencement ceremony for the North Chennai Thermal Power Station at that very site. But because of the two-year delay, the Rs. 500 crore project became a Rs. 700 crore project and has now grown to a scale of Rs. 1,000 or Rs. 1,200 crore. Thus it was under Kazhagam rule, immediately after we returned to office, that the North Chennai Thermal Power Station was begun. Today it is functioning.
At the existing Ranipet complex, a second-phase industrial complex was established on 113 acres — a further 113 acres — and through it employment has been provided to 3,400 people.

Similarly, the second-phase Hosur industrial complex was established on 457 acres with investment of nearly Rs. 1,000 crore. Six thousand young people have obtained employment there. Expansion on 800 acres at Gummidipoondi was then planned. A similar complex was planned at Perundurai in Periyar district. In the Nellai-Kattabomman district, a 2,000-acre complex of this kind for engineering was planned at Gangaikondan. When all these projects were about to be implemented, the Kazhagam Government was dismissed for the second time. After that dismissal, were any efforts made during the past five years to implement the announced projects at Perundurai, Gangaikondan—

and the other proposed complexes? Not only those connected with them but everyone in Tamil Nadu knows that there were none. It was in 1989-90, when the Kazhagam Government was in office, that the following Joint Sector companies were created and began production: ‘Evian Paints’, with an investment of Rs. 22 crore; ‘Telecommunications Consultant India Limited’, with an investment of Rs. 29 crore; and Tiruchirappalli ‘S. S. Sankarareddy Associates’, with an investment of Rs. 10 crore. The Kazhagam Government also planned through TIDCO a factory costing Rs. 140 crore to manufacture ‘titanium dioxide’.

It was just when we had once again begun systematically planning and working energetically for industrial growth in Tamil Nadu that, as I said earlier, the Kazhagam Government was dismissed. We are almost afraid even to draw up plans to increase industrial development, because whenever we draw up plans, they sharpen the knife to dismiss the Kazhagam Government.

I should also point out industries that recovered from sickness under Kazhagam rule. Tamil Nadu Minerals Development Corporation, which had become sick because of administrative disorder, earned a profit of Rs. 4 crore as a result of reform measures taken by the Kazhagam Government in 1989-90. The Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers company had continuously suffered losses up to 1989, losses of around Rs. 49 to 50 crore. But the Kazhagam Government restructured the company and raised it, within a single year, to the level of earning a net profit of Rs. 28 crore. (Sound of desk-thumping.) I say this with great happiness.
I referred at the outset to the granite policy. The granite policy had already become utterly chaotic, a situation in which anyone could dominate and anyone could loot.

During Kazhagam rule in 1989-90, we took action to make the policy for granting mineral-quarrying rights uniform and introduced the tender system. In those two years, by tendering quarries at 103 locations covering a total of 272 hectares, the Government received nearly Rs. 20 crore in revenue. I have explained many times in this House what happened under the Government that followed after the Kazhagam Government was dismissed, and I do not wish to go into it in detail again.

The tender system was changed. The tender system is a method capable of operating fairly and honestly, a method praised and appreciated by everyone. When Jayalalitha assumed office as Chief Minister and a Government was formed under her leadership, this very tender system was changed and a procedure called Rule 39 was introduced. As a result, in the three-year period from 1993 to April 1996, Government revenue from quarry leases was only Rs. 5.12 crore. Under Kazhagam rule in 1989-90, the Government had earlier received Rs. 20 crore. But from 1993 to 1996, over three years, revenue was only Rs. 5.12 crore because the system had been changed.

In an inquiry conducted by the Vigilance Task Force and the ‘Vigilance Commission’ in this connection, it was estimated that because proper procedures had not been followed in granting leases during the previous Government and lease amounts had not been collected, the Government suffered a revenue loss of between Rs. 70 crore and Rs. 95 crore. After the Kazhagam Government again assumed office in 1996, Rule 39 was removed and it was announced that the quotation/tender system would again be followed. Today that activity is running profitably; I shall announce the amount of profit at the appropriate stage when the next announcement is made.
Similarly, this Government has amended Rules 8 and 8-A relating to jelly and minor minerals such as sand and has reintroduced the tender system.

As an example of the result of this procedural change, I shall take only Coimbatore district, because I have not yet received the accounts for all districts. In Coimbatore district alone, last year’s income — the income obtained under that Government — was Rs. 2.88 lakh. That is, the revenue from minor minerals such as jelly and sand was Rs. 2.88 lakh in Coimbatore district alone. This year, Rs. 26.17 lakh has been received in Coimbatore district alone. (Sound of desk-thumping.) I ask you to think about how much had been looted. Under the old system they had maintained, the old system without tenders, they collected Rs. 2.88 lakh; because we have newly changed that same system, the amount we are to receive is Rs. 67.32 lakh in Coimbatore district alone. I wish to state that this is on the basis of the new change.

It is not merely that the Industries Department had been neglected irresponsibly; a policy had been established about whom entrepreneurs had to “look after”, and industry had been ruined from the roots. This is not said by me, but in the report of a research unit called the “Economist Intelligence Unit”, in an article titled “India uncaged”, “Seeking opportunities in the South”, published in November 1995. It says: “The Report says - “If there is any State. . .” — look carefully — “If there is any State with a reputation for corruption, it is Tamil Nadu”. If there is any—

State that can be said to excel in corruption, the State with that reputation is Tamil Nadu. When? In 1995. Who says it? Not Karunanidhi, but a research report. The Economist Intelligence Unit research report says: “The going rate for back handers in the form of commission is said to be about 10 to 15 percent of even the project cost”. A major article was published after researching that 10 to 15 per cent of the estimate, of the cost of every project, had to be paid as commission to those who stood in between and arranged matters. No further example is needed to show how Tamil Nadu’s fame had risen, grown and stood high in 1995.

That is precisely why, so that no such blemishes or defects should come to this Government or to Tamil Nadu, our tenders must be open, a situation must be created in which anyone can obtain information about them, and that opportunity must be available to them. The Industries Department is proceeding in that manner today. A high-level committee has also been constituted to give advice required for industrial development; experienced industrialists, Government officials and young entrepreneurs are members, and the committee meets frequently and gives the Government the advice it needs.

Because of this Government’s industry-friendly policies — ‘Industry-Friendly Policies’ — and its open, transparent — ‘transparent appoach’ — approach, many new industries are coming up in Tamil Nadu. In ten months, opportunities have arisen for many industries to begin. I wish to place before you only a few of them—
though you may already have heard of them from time to time, because it is my duty to present them together.

A floriculture (Flori-Culture) project through Blooming Meadows Limited, with 100 per cent export, is being established at Hosur at an estimated cost of Rs. 33 crore. A project costing Rs. 35 crore to manufacture products using fly ash is planned at Ennore through the “Fly Ashbest Blocks” company. A 100 per cent export meat-processing project costing Rs. 169 crore is being started near Pollachi. A modern integrated coconut-products manufacturing project costing Rs. 38.42 crore is to be started near Pollachi.

A glass factory is to be established at Singaperumalkoil by the British Pilkington company at an estimated cost of Rs. 450 crore. A glass factory of Tamil Nadu Telecom is to be established at Maraimalai Nagar at a cost of Rs. 40 crore.

Ashok Leyland has begun a project to expand its Hosur division at an estimated cost of Rs. 630 crore and produce 10,000 lorries a year. A permanent trade centre is to be established on 35 acres near Chennai airport. South Korea’s Kumho Tyres is establishing a tyre factory at an estimated cost of Rs. 350 crore. South Korea’s Hyundai Motor company is establishing a car factory in the Irungattukottai SIPCOT industrial complex at an estimated cost of Rs. 2450 crore.
A carbon-black factory costing Rs. 115 crore has been established by Hitech in the Gummidipoondi SIPCOT industrial complex.
Hindustan Motors, in collaboration with Japan’s Mitsubishi company, is establishing at Tiruvallur a factory costing Rs. 300 crore to manufacture the Lancer car.

A note about the establishment of such large industries. A distinguished journalist named Mark Nicholson wrote a major article in *Financial Time*, 10 April 1997. He wrote: “Tamil Nadu car industry is perhaps the most spectacular result of the race between States to attract foreign investment and develop new industries”. He thus noted that Tamil Nadu’s car industry was growing to a very high level of results, competing with other States, and went on to say: “Tamil Nadu does not yet produce one finished car” — not even one finished car is yet being produced. But: “But within three years new production lines near Madras will roll out 2,44,000 a year”. He said it would grow to a level capable of producing 2,44,000 cars a year. He then says: “I don't think anywhere else in the world at this point offers this level of opportunities to the British component industry”, says Mr. Bernard Fintlay, International Trade Manager for the British Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, recently on reconnaissance in Madras”.

Such praise of the car factories now approved and being established in Tamil Nadu has appeared in the press. I have read out here only a few passages from the article by that distinguished reporter under the heading — “Madras revs up to achieve car ambitions” - Tamil Nadu State is profiting from India's liberalised Industry policy, writes Mark Nicholson”.

Further, our Thiru Tha. Kiruttinan has often spoken here about establishing the Tamil Nadu Graphite Limited graphite factory. Thiru Chidambaram, who was, and is going to be, Finance Minister at the Centre, has taken great interest in it and has also been involved in the work relating to it.

A company has now been started to consult experienced advisers (Consultants) on identifying the graphite ore available in the Sivaganga area and creating an industrial unit. That company has been formed under the name Tamil Nadu Graphite Limited and is engaged in those studies. The issue is that the total graphite mineral reserve in that area of Sivaganga is estimated at 35.41 lakh tonnes. The graphite there is 14 per cent pure. A plan has been drawn up and discussions are being held with consultants to raise it to 96 per cent purity. I therefore assure the House that the Government will energetically complete the preliminary arrangements required for the graphite factory to come up, and I wish to place a few announcements before the House.

A Bill concerning a Single Window Clearance system, under which all licences needed to start industries can be issued at one place, has already been placed before the Legislative Assembly. After this Bill becomes law, Industrial Townships will be created in all industrial centres. To administer those Industrial Townships, administrative—
authorities — Executive Authority — will be established. These administrative authorities will function as bodies empowered to issue immediately all licences required for industrial development.

After sand, jelly and mineral-soil quarries have been properly leased by District Collectors and Geology Department officials, responsibility for supervising quarry operations will henceforth be given to local bodies so that there are no irregularities in transporting minerals from quarries and so that the full revenue due to local bodies reaches them. (Sound of desk-thumping.) Accordingly, every time a Load — a load of goods — is taken from a quarry, the relevant mineral charge (Seigniorage fee) must first be paid into the local body’s bank account. Only after that, and only with the vehicle permit (Transport Permit) issued by the local body, will a lorry be allowed to proceed with the load. (Sound of desk-thumping.) The responsibility for issuing the permit must be handled jointly by the Panchayat President with either the Vice-President or another member. By giving this responsibility to the Panchayat, illegal transport of sand, jelly and similar materials will be prevented and the Panchayat’s revenue will also increase.

There is difficulty in obtaining enough trained workers for newly emerging factories. Therefore, in order to meet the need for trained workers, this Government will take steps to start Industrial Training Institutes (I.T.I.s) in large numbers. As a result, many young people will receive proper training in various industrial-training trades and obtain employment in new factories coming up. I am happy to inform the House that immediately after this Government assumed office, it decided to establish one I.T.I. in every Panchayat Union and that the scheme is being implemented.

The Government has decided to start four new Joint Sector projects using granite stone, each covering 50 hectares, together covering 200 hectares, for industries based on granite. I inform you that quotations for these projects will soon be invited through the proper procedure.

When Thiru Subbarayan spoke, he pointed out that when each industry is started, consideration must be given to what the environmental situation will be; otherwise, problems will arise after it begins. Tanning, dyeing, foundry, stone-breaking and several other industries had continuously discharged waste indiscriminately without concern for environmental protection. Following a recent court judgment regarding the environmental damage caused by this, difficulties have arisen in continuing these industries.

To remove these difficulties and help such factories function effectively again, this Government plans to establish new industrial complexes with all facilities in suburban areas. Separate divisions will be created within them as tannery park complexes, dyeing-industry park complexes, leather-goods industrial park complexes and foundry-industry park complexes, and waste-treatment facilities suited to the respective industries will be provided.
When I say electronic parks, electronic parks, you should not imagine a flower garden. They are also called industrial parks. At that—

level, to keep pace with the rapid growth taking place in electronics, quotations have been invited to establish Technology Parks at Kelambakkam in Chennai and at Coimbatore. Likewise, this Government has planned to establish two Software Techno Parks, one near Chennai and one at Madurai.

New industrial centres: keeping in view the growing industrial opportunities and the need to provide proper employment to the youth community, this Government has planned to start new industrial centres in suburban Chennai, along the National Highway in Villupuram Ramasamy Padayatchiyar district, in Coimbatore district and in Dharmapuri district. I am happy to inform you of this. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Tamil Nadu’s future electricity dreams depend to a large extent on the gas project called L.N.G. (Liquified Natural Gas). For that LNG project, an LNG terminal will be established at Ennore, where 2 million tonnes of liquefied gas brought by ship will be stored. Nearby, in the first phase, a 2,500-megawatt power station will be built. The gas in liquid form will be converted back to gaseous form and sent through pipelines to the power-generation station, where electricity will be produced.

The first-stage cost of this enormous project is Rs. 12,000 crore. Where can we go in the public sector for this Rs. 12,000 crore? Therefore, those who have come forward saying they are ready to take up and implement the tenders issued for it are—
1. Mobil L.N.G., U.S.A.
2. Shell International Gas, England.
3. Coastal Gas Corporation, U.S.A.
4. Amoga Power Resources Corporation, U.S.A.
5. Phillips Petroleum Company, U.S.A.
6. Occidental company, U.S.A.
7. Gas de France, France.
8. Total, France.
9. Niso Iwai, Japan.
10. Marubeni Corporation, Japan.
11. Glenak Engineering Group, Australia.
12. Imperial SDN BHD, Malaysia.
13. Reliance Power Limited, Mumbai.

They have come forward with interest to participate in the contract and implement the project. One among them will get the project. I am very happy to inform this House that Tamil Nadu is soon going to obtain a magnificent project. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

There has been a criticism that many large industrial projects are developing only around Chennai. To avoid congestion, the Industries Department will establish a satellite town on 2,000 acres near Sriperumbudur, where the Hyundai car factory is coming up, and another satellite town in the Singaperumalkoil area, where the Ford car factory is coming up—
on 500 acres. I inform you that these two satellite towns will be used to change, to some extent, the situation in which industries are created only in Chennai. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Already, when the Kazhagam Government was in office in 1989-90-91, a private knitwear industrial estate — a banian industrial estate — was planned at Mudalipalayam adjoining Tiruppur, and everyone knows that the work was completed within a short period. Likewise, if private parties come together to create industrial centres with all facilities, it has been planned to extend to them all the concessions given to factories in industrial estates established by the Government.

The Government has decided to give appropriate assistance to entrepreneurs who come forward to manufacture brick-like construction material (Construction Blocks) using fly ash discharged from thermal power stations at Ennore, Tuticorin, Mettur, Neyveli and North Chennai.

The Jayankondam coal company: this is a major problem that has remained unresolved for a long time. The Jayankondam Coal Company, registered in 1991, has remained merely at the announcement stage without being started because of the approach of the previous Government. Agreements made under the previous Government for mining the coal and supplying the required machinery, without inviting tenders, have been cancelled by this Government. When that Government was preparing to entrust work for the Jayankondam Coal Company without calling tenders, this Government assumed office. Those agreements were then cancelled. Tenders have now been invited from companies willing to supply, each year—
4 million tonnes of coal and 500 megawatts of electricity at a low price. I am certain that a dawn will come for this project this year. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

The Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce in Singapore has agreed to function as a window (Window), giving entrepreneurs in Singapore information about investing in Tamil Nadu, which I am happy to inform you. A team consisting of our Government officials and entrepreneurs was sent to Singapore, where they held discussions and obtained agreement from those there. An agreement has also been entered into with this organisation for the purpose. I am duty-bound to say with great happiness that these efforts will serve as an incentive for investment by Singapore companies to reach Tamil Nadu.

TIDCO’s new projects: a petrochemical park will be established on about 7,000 acres around the new Ennore Port. Treatment plants will be set up there to purify wastewater and turn it into good water for reuse.
An egg-processing project at an estimated cost of Rs. 40 crore will be implemented in collaboration with the S.K.M. Group.
In collaboration with National Plywood Limited and Germany’s Siempelkamp company, a project costing Rs. 150 crore will be implemented to manufacture small boards from sugarcane—
bagasse.
A project will be implemented to manufacture chemical products based on alcohol.
In collaboration with Norway’s Norske Hydro, a project will be implemented to manufacture raw materials needed for P.V.C. pipes. I also inform you that the agreement for this was signed last month.
A Naphtha Crackers & Olefins complex will be established with an investment of Rs. 7,500 crore.

At the Chennai Export Zone, a project costing Rs. 27 crore, with 100 per cent export and capable of being implemented in the Associate Sector, is to be started for the manufacture of metal tube lamps (halide lamps).

As many floriculture projects are being implemented in the Hosur area, a centre costing Rs. 75 crore, with cold-storage facilities, refrigerated-vehicle facilities and other amenities, will be established there to encourage those projects.

In collaboration with TIDCO, a factory estimated at Rs. 325 crore will be established to manufacture East Poly Propylene, Biaxially oriented poly propylene - (Bopp), Bisphenol-A (Bisphenol-A), and activated carbon.

Through the renowned Lakshmi Machine Works and TIDCO’s associate company Siscal (Siscal), a pig-iron factory has been started with an investment of Rs. 450 crore. I also inform you that the iron factory, valued at Rs. 210 crore, will begin production around January next year.

Sterlite has begun production at its copper factory in Tuticorin with an investment of Rs. 1,000 crore. There were objections to that factory. On the basis of the efforts taken by the Government because of those objections — that the factory should function, but that people and fishermen should not be affected by waste coming from the factory — all those difficulties have been resolved and the factory has been started, which I wish to inform you.
A Bulk Drug Intermediates factory will be established at Manali in the Joint Sector at a cost of Rs. 50 crore.
An industrial-enzyme factory will be started with an investment of Rs. 70 crore.
Through ‘Tansam’, the Government has planned to start this year at Virudhachalam a factory costing Rs. 1.4 crore to produce 1,920 tonnes a year of high-grade aluminium stones.

Our Hon. member Mani and our Hon. member Moses spoke about the rubber industry in Kanyakumari and asked how they could go back home. You may go back boldly. For many years I too have been trying to ensure that a rubber factory must somehow come there. Because it is a rubber factory, it keeps stretching on. (Laughter.) Therefore, this year I will make the effort saying, “I will not leave it; I will not touch it,” so that the factory somehow comes; that will be my first task. I inform the people and members of Kanyakumari of this. (Sound of desk-thumping.)

Similarly, Tmt. Kanchana Kamalanathan said that everything is being given only to those in the front row and that she is sitting at the back. I ask all of them only this: you may remain at the back, but do not remain backward. With the confidence that they will no longer remain backward, I give the assurance that the mango factory will certainly be established at Krishnagiri.

With this, I convey my thanks and appreciation to everyone who spoke and gave their views on this grant. I request all members to withdraw the cut motions and approve the amount sought under this grant, and I take my seat. Thank you. Greetings. (Sound of desk-thumping.)
